title: India’s competitive coexistence with China
gist: India's apparent thaw with China — Modi's SCO trip, Jaishankar–Wang Yi talks in Manila, Misri's Beijing visit, and a possible Xi visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit — is not a return to the pre-Galwan relationship but a deliberate strategy of 'competitive coexistence': restoring practical engagement while treating rivalry as permanent. Supply-chain diversification, Quad alignment and border deterrence all remain in place, and the re-engagement is driven partly by trade friction with Washington that has shown India partnerships do not eliminate divergent interests.

insights.claim: India has drawn an operational distinction between normalising engagement and normalising relations with China, meaning diplomatic and practical cooperation can be restored without any restoration of trust.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Read India–China headlines through this filter: resumed flights, visas and trade channels are not evidence of strategic realignment, and should not be extrapolated into a softening of India's China-restriction policies.
insights.quote: New Delhi appears to have concluded that there is a difference between normalising engagement and normalising relations.

insights.claim: New Delhi is not seeking to restore its pre-Galwan relationship with China but to build a framework for managing a rivalry it regards as permanent.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Anyone pricing a durable India–China détente — for supply chains, tariffs on Chinese goods, or investment approvals — is likely mispricing the ceiling on this relationship.
insights.quote: A better reading is that India is not seeking to restore its pre-Galwan relationship with China, but it is trying to build a framework for managing a rivalry it sees as permanent.

insights.claim: India's operating premise is that China is a rival that cannot be ignored, isolated or transformed, so engagement must proceed without waiting for a comprehensive political settlement.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Implies an indefinite regime of partial cooperation plus persistent restrictions — a structurally noisy but rarely rupturing bilateral, rather than a binary reset-or-conflict outcome.
insights.quote: China is a rival that cannot be ignored, isolated or transformed.
insights.locator: New Delhi has accepted a more durable reality

insights.claim: Jaishankar paired talks on restoring practical cooperation with a public restatement that border peace is a precondition for normal ties, encapsulating an approach of expanding engagement while withholding normalisation.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: The border remains the explicit gating condition — any Line of Actual Control incident can freeze the practical-cooperation track without warning.
insights.quote: peace and tranquillity in the border areas is obviously the prerequisite for normal ties
insights.locator: During his meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Manila

insights.claim: The 2020 Galwan clash broke the implicit bargain that had held since the 1993 Line of Actual Control agreement, under which India and China insulated cooperation from an unresolved boundary dispute for nearly three decades.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: The pre-2020 compartmentalisation model is gone; assume border risk now transmits directly into trade, investment and tech policy rather than being firewalled off.
insights.quote: Their boundary dispute remained unresolved, but both governments sought to prevent it from disrupting cooperation elsewhere.
insights.locator: For nearly three decades after the 1993 Agreement

insights.claim: None of India's post-Galwan structural measures have been reversed: scrutiny of Chinese investment, intensified Quad cooperation, a more security-focused Indo-Pacific strategy, supply-chain diversification and domestic manufacturing support all remain in force.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Chinese capital and components should not be modelled as regaining easy access to India on the back of the diplomatic thaw; the China+1 manufacturing shift into India retains policy backing.
insights.quote: None of these factors have changed (Opens in new window) in the last couple of years.
insights.locator: Chinese investment came under greater scrutiny

insights.claim: India continues to treat China's expanding maritime presence as an unresolved concern even while restoring diplomatic channels.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Naval and maritime-domain-awareness spending in India stays on an upward path irrespective of diplomatic atmospherics.
insights.locator: India has not reduced its concerns

insights.claim: India will simultaneously strengthen border deterrence and restore selected diplomatic channels — a two-track 'managed rivalry' rather than a choice between balancing and engagement.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Expect Indian defence procurement and border infrastructure to keep expanding through periods of visible diplomatic warmth — the two are not substitutes.
insights.quote: This amounts to a strategy of managed rivalry.
insights.locator: If that is true, then engagement cannot wait

insights.claim: Trade frictions with Washington, including new tariff measures and disagreements over economic policy, have pushed New Delhi to widen its diplomatic options rather than rely on a single partnership.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: US tariff escalation on India has a measurable second-order cost: it directly increases Indian incentives to re-open Beijing channels, weakening US leverage in the Indo-Pacific.
insights.quote: Trade frictions with Washington (Opens in new window), including the latest tariff measures and renewed disagreements over economic policy, have reminded New Delhi that partnerships do not eliminate divergent interests.
insights.locator: India’s external environment has also become more uncertain

insights.claim: Framing India's China re-engagement as hedging between Washington and Beijing misreads it — India is hedging against uncertainty about China's own future behaviour, not against US–China competition.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: The 'India is drifting to Beijing' narrative is the wrong trade; India's alignment with US-led security structures is not the variable being adjusted here.
insights.quote: If India is hedging, it is hedging against uncertainty about China’s future behaviour rather than against competition between great powers.
insights.locator: In that regard, many will interpret

insights.claim: A Xi Jinping visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit would be his first trip to India since 2019 and the first since the Galwan clash reset the relationship.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: A concrete, dateable catalyst next month for headline risk-on sentiment in India–China trade and travel-linked names, without implying structural change.
insights.locator: If China’s President Xi Jinping travels

insights.claim: China has front-loaded practical confidence-building measures ahead of the BRICS summit, including resumed border trade through Nathu La, Lipulekh and Shipki La plus talks on direct flights, visas and institutional exchanges.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: These are the specific, verifiable deliverables to track as the real gauge of thaw depth — direct flight resumption and visa liberalisation are the tradeable ones.
insights.quote: including the resumption of border trade (Opens in new window) through Nathu La, Lipulekh and Shipki La, alongside discussions on direct flights, visas, and institutional exchanges
insights.locator: China has signalled a willingness to stabilise

insights.claim: India and China want structurally different things from BRICS: Beijing treats it as a vehicle for expanding influence in global governance while New Delhi wants a more representative order and preserves its own autonomy.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Caps the plausible ambition of BRICS-wide initiatives — de-dollarisation or bloc-style alignment projects face an Indian brake from inside the chair's seat.
insights.quote: China views BRICS as a vehicle for expanding its influence (Opens in new window) within global governance, whereas India supports a more representative international order, remaining committed to its autonomy.
insights.locator: China views BRICS as a vehicle

insights.claim: India's BRICS chairmanship this year gives New Delhi an added institutional incentive to prevent competition with Beijing from derailing multilateral cooperation.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Expect India to actively suppress India–China escalation through end-2026 for chairmanship reasons — a calendar-bounded stabiliser that may lapse afterwards.

insights.claim: China remains India's largest neighbour and a major trading partner whose participation is indispensable on climate change, regional stability and multilateral institutions, which is why engagement cannot be conditioned on settling the political dispute.
insights.speaker: Sanchari Ghosh
insights.so_what: Bilateral trade dependence gives the relationship a hard floor — full decoupling is not the base case even under renewed border stress.
insights.quote: engagement cannot wait for a comprehensive political settlement. It has to occur despite the absence of one.
